title: R.I.P. Geomean Speedup Use Equal-Work (Or Equal-Time) Harmonic Mean Speedup Instead
problem: Geometric mean speedup, the dominant metric for summarizing multi-workload performance in computer architecture research, is mathematically ill-defined for speedup ratios and produces incorrect average speedup values that can lead to wrong architectural conclusions.
motivation: The widespread misuse of geometric mean speedup in architecture papers has silently biased comparative evaluations, because the geometric mean does not preserve the correct total-work or total-time interpretation that speedup ratios require.
method: The paper derives harmonic mean speedup from two concrete scenarios: equal-work (how much faster one system finishes the same task) and equal-time (how much more work gets done in the same time). It proves that harmonic mean correctly averages performance across multiple workloads, while the currently-used geometric mean does not. Examples show geometric and harmonic mean can rank competing architectures oppositely, so the wrong metric leads to wrong architectural choices.
key_novelty: Equal-work harmonic mean speedup is the mathematically correct metric for summarizing system performance across multiple workloads.
contributions: Proof that geometric mean speedup is mathematically meaningless for summarizing speedups across workloads.
Definition of equal-work and equal-time harmonic mean speedup metrics with explicit, transparent assumptions.
Demonstration with real examples that the choice of averaging method changes architectural conclusions.
Recommendation that equal-work harmonic mean speedup should replace geomean speedup in architecture research.
limitations: The paper focuses on speedup ratios and does not extend the analysis to energy-delay product, throughput/watt, or other composite metrics.
primary_theme: Correct statistical methodology for reporting aggregate speedup in computer architecture
